confidence_note: Written from knowledge of the book; no page-level check. Core: 10 May 1996, Everest summit day for Adventure Consultants (Rob Hall) and Mountain Madness (Scott Fischer); a 2 p.m. turnaround time was set; many climbers were above it; client Doug Hansen reached the summit after 4 p.m. with Hall; a storm hit; eight climbers died over 10-11 May including Hall, Fischer and Hansen. Omitted on purpose: Krakauer's own summit time, names of other dead, exact times of the storm, oxygen figures, his explanations beyond the turnaround rule. Added from memory of Krakauer, not page-checked: Krakauer's summit time, bottleneck and late ropes, Hansen's job, 1995 turnback, satellite call.
facts: On 10 May 1996 two commercial expeditions, led by Rob Hall and Scott Fischer, climbed Everest on the same day; Krakauer was in Hall's group.
The guides had set a turnaround time of 2 p.m.: anyone not on the summit by then was supposed to turn back.
Many climbers were still climbing after 2 p.m.
Hall's client Doug Hansen reached the summit after 4 p.m., and Hall stayed with him.
Eight people died on the mountain on 10 and 11 May, including Hall, Fischer and Hansen.
Krakauer links the disaster to decisions on the mountain, including the failure to enforce the turnaround time.
Krakauer reached the summit before 2 p.m. and started down; queues and late fixed ropes slowed climbers near the top.
Hansen was a postal worker; Hall had turned him back a year earlier; Hall spoke by satellite phone with his pregnant wife Jan Arnold.
scene_details: a rule: 2 p.m. summit or turn back
a client reaching the top after 4 p.m.
tension: A turnaround time everyone had agreed on was passed by hours.
opening_idea: Open on 2 p.m., the hour set for turning back, and the climbers still going up.

lessons.idea: Set a stopping rule before the push and decide who enforces it.
lessons.anchor: the 2 p.m. turnaround time was set but not kept

reflect_final: Which project or purchase has a point where you should stop, and what rule could you write down now so it is not decided in the heat of the moment?

use_cases.situation: A project is over budget, but the team says it is nearly done.
use_cases.move: Mention the 2 p.m. turnaround rule on Everest and ask what limit was agreed at the start.

use_cases.situation: You are about to push on a long drive because you are close.
use_cases.move: Agree with your passenger on a time to stop and check it.

use_cases.situation: You are deep into a goal and not sure of your limit.
use_cases.move: Write the stopping point on a card today.

pocket_idea: On Everest the turnaround time was 2 p.m. and it was passed: write your stopping rule before the push.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: On Everest in 1996 the turnaround time was 2 p.m., and a client was still reaching the summit after 4.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: On 10 May 1996 guides on Everest had set a 2 p.m. turnaround time. Many climbers were still climbing after that, and Rob Hall stayed with his client Doug Hansen, who reached the summit after 4. A storm came that evening, and eight people died over the two days. Jon Krakauer, who was there, ties it to decisions, including keeping that rule only on paper.
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: rule on paper, rule in practice
